records.name: Saint Barthélemy
records.current_summary:
Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on ~40 referrals since 2010, it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Travel guide: 'full equality' under French law on ~8 square miles and ~10,000 residents; luxury-yacht economy long welcoming to gay couples with zero visible scene — discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10 (9 positive rights, 1 red flag): legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access; no government LGBT+ travel advice (FCDO shows no warnings); no trans-specific visitor tips yet submitted.

Luxury-operator guide: low crime, open and accepting culture with no Pride-specific events, staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet — no LGBTQ venues or scene, but no hostility noted.

freshness_all.fact: French framework applies: marriage equality, anti-discrimination law and the 2023 conversion-practice ban; local acceptance lower, no legal regression.

records.name: Aruba
records.current_summary:
An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Netherlands; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

records.name: Curaçao
records.current_summary:
Also an autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, the island's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction: representatives of all kingdom governments agreed in 2015 on an equal-rights package for Caribbean-country LGBT residents — yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the island's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.

Travel-culture surveys place the island inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. The record is brief; what exists shows institutions contested rather than hostile.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Netherlands; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

records.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
records.current_summary:
These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are the kingdom's own, and they are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Netherlands; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GayCities (14 Dec 2022, updated 1 Sep 2023): 'Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in the Caribbean and Latin America' ranks Bonaire at #5 — as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws, same-sex couples are warmly welcomed; notes Bonaire uses the US dollar. For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

Saba Tourism official weddings page: the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony is the Court Room in the Administrative Building; registrar Julieta Woods is documented as flexible with couples' wishes; full destination-wedding infrastructure (caterers, flowers, accommodations). For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

freshness_all.fact: Dutch equality law applies to the public bodies; same-sex marriage performed on Bonaire/Sint Eustatius/Saba since 2018; no later change found.

records.name: Faroe Islands
records.current_summary:
A self-governing archipelago in the Realm of Denmark: domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after church-state friction. Nothing in the audited record criminalises trans people or documents enforcement against them.

The climate is measured by politics rather than prosecution: in 2006 activists gathered some 20,000 signatures — a large share of a ~50,000 population — demanding anti-discrimination protection after surveys found violence and discrimination against out gay people 'not uncommon' and legally unaddressed; a Centre Party MP who refused to share a state banquet with Iceland's gay premier (2010, 'a direct provocation') was still demanding Pride bans in 2015, when a nationally beloved singer urged the public to ignore him. For a visitor: low violence risk, thin legal protection, and high-profile political hostility to visibility.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Denmark; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: PinkNews (9 Nov 2006): LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at the time the Faroes (population ~47,000, self-governing within Denmark) had neither protection, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

Gay Iceland (Jul 2015): when Faroese MP Jenis av Rana demanded Pride be banned (held two days before the national holiday), singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality — documents anti-Pride pressure and organised public pushback.

records.name: Greenland
records.current_summary:
A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.

For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010 and a national equality association (Qaamaneq, 2014). The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: some 56,000 people across remote settlements means thin institutional reach, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Denmark; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz 'Gay Greenland - Past and Present' (May 2015): gay life is 'almost a non-event' — low-key, integrated, non-violent; modest Pride march since 2010; the 1996 same-sex partnership law passed with virtually no debate — a picture of quiet tolerance.

PinkNews (Apr 2016): Greenland's same-sex marriage law came into effect — adopted Danish legislation, passed unanimously twice (first bill lapsed due to Danish elections); replaces the 1996 partnership law; the established church's bishop supported it.

KNR Greenlandic Broadcasting (Aug 2014): new national association LGBT Qaamaneq founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people — political, cultural and social equality, open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

records.name: Puerto Rico
records.current_summary:
A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United States; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: NCTE airport-security guide for trans travelers: all luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics (incl. breast forms) are treated as medically necessary and not subject to the 3-liquid rule; medical equipment/prosthetics allowed through checkpoint after screening; advises packing strategies to reduce invasive searches. Applies at PR airports as federal TSA procedure - the framework a trans visitor actually stands under.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report.

records.name: Guam
records.current_summary:
An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

Academic Pacific-identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents. The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, federal volatility amplified by the base, and small-island visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United States; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: A4TE 'Know Your Rights: Airport Security': TSA body-scanner and pat-down procedures can 'out' trans travellers; the guide covers pre-flight packing, document/screening mismatches, the right to request alternative screening, and how to escalate airport problems. Notes most trans travellers pass screening without incident. In scope for Guam as a US-territory TSA jurisdiction — visitor-facing screening guidance.
